name: Swift
year_note: Chris Lattner began the language in secret at Apple in July 2010; it was unveiled at WWDC on 2 June 2014 and reached 1.0 on 9 September 2014. It was open-sourced, with a Linux port, on 3 December 2015.
tagline: Apple's safe, fast successor to Objective-C, built on value types, protocols, optionals and automatic reference counting.
summary: Swift is a compiled, statically typed, multi-paradigm language created by Apple to replace Objective-C on its platforms, and open source since 2015. It emphasises safety — optionals instead of null pointers, definite initialisation, bounds- and overflow-checked arithmetic — while compiling to native code through LLVM and interoperating directly with C and Objective-C (and, since Swift 5.9, C++). Idiomatic Swift favours value types and 'protocol-oriented programming', and Swift 5.5 through 6 built async/await, actors and compile-time data-race checking into the language.
history:
Chris Lattner, the original author of LLVM, started work on Swift at Apple in July 2010 and implemented much of the basic language in secret; other engineers began contributing in earnest late in 2011, and in July 2013 it became a major focus of Apple's developer tools group. Swift was motivated by the need to replace Objective-C, whose design dated from the early 1980s, and drew ideas "from Objective-C, Rust, Haskell, Ruby, Python, C#, CLU, and far too many others to list". Apple unveiled it at WWDC on 2 June 2014 — the conference's own app was the first publicly released app written in Swift — and 1.0 followed in September.

The language changed quickly and source-incompatibly through Swift 3 (2016). Swift 2 (2015) added a throws/try/catch error model and protocol extensions, the basis of the 'protocol-oriented programming' style, and on 3 December 2015 the compiler, standard library and package manager were open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 licence with a Linux port. Lattner left Apple in January 2017 and Ted Kremenek became project lead. Swift 5 (2019) made the ABI stable on Apple platforms, the same year SwiftUI introduced a declarative UI framework; Swift 5.5 (2021) added async/await and actors, Swift 5.9 (2023) macros, parameter packs and noncopyable types, and Swift 6 (2024) compile-time data-race safety.
innovations: Protocol-oriented programming: protocol extensions with default implementations, retroactive conformance and value types as an alternative to class hierarchies
Optionals with dedicated syntax (T?, optional chaining, if let / guard let, ??) at the centre of a mainstream application language
Deterministic automatic reference counting, inherited from Objective-C, as the memory model of a mainstream language with no tracing GC
Direct interoperability with C and Objective-C (and later C++), letting large codebases migrate file by file
ABI stability with library evolution, so OS frameworks written in Swift can change without apps being recompiled
Actor isolation and Sendable checking that turn data races into compile-time errors (Swift 6 language mode)
Result builders and property wrappers that enable declarative embedded DSLs such as SwiftUI

typing.notes: Bidirectional, expression-level inference; function signatures are annotated. Protocol conformance is declared (nominal) but can be added retroactively in extensions. Integer overflow traps unless the &+ family of operators is used.

influenced_by.note: Designed as its replacement on Apple platforms: on Darwin it shares the Objective-C runtime and Cocoa APIs; ARC, protocols, extensions (categories) and keyword-labelled arguments carry over.

influenced_by_external.name: D
influenced_by_external.note: Listed as an influence in Wikipedia's infobox.

structured-control.note: `guard` for early exit; `switch` does not fall through and must be exhaustive.

exceptions.note: throws/try/do-catch, implemented as ordinary return paths rather than stack unwinding; typed throws since Swift 6.

coroutines.note: async functions are implemented as coroutines that suspend at `await`.

generators.note: Sequence/IteratorProtocol drive for-in and `lazy` gives lazy adapters (map/filter on arrays are eager); AsyncSequence since 5.5; no `yield`-based generator functions.

pattern-matching.note: `switch`/`if case` with enum, tuple, optional and value-binding patterns plus `where` guards.

generics.note: Constrained generics, opaque `some P` types (5.1) and variadic parameter packs (5.9).

algebraic-data-types.note: Enums with associated values (recursive via `indirect`); structs and tuples as products.

type-classes.note: Protocols with associated types, conditional and retroactive conformances resolved statically for generics.

option-types.note: Optional<T> spelled T?, with ?. chaining, ?? defaults and if let / guard let unwrapping.

ownership.note: Opt-in: noncopyable types (~Copyable) and borrowing/consuming parameter modifiers; ordinary values remain copyable and ARC-managed.

interfaces.note: Protocols, adopted by classes, structs and enums alike.

classes.note: Reference-type classes alongside value-type structs and enums.

inheritance.note: Single class inheritance with `override` and `final`; structs and enums cannot inherit, and protocols are preferred.

traits-mixins.note: Protocol extensions supply default implementations to every conforming type.

abstract-data-types.note: Access levels open, public, package (Swift 5.9), internal, fileprivate and private.

modules.note: Each target is a module with no header files; Swift Package Manager since 2015.

operator-overloading.note: Operators can be overloaded and new infix/prefix/postfix operators declared with precedence groups.

closures.note: Trailing-closure syntax, $0 shorthand arguments and explicit capture lists.

immutability.note: `let` versus `var` is chosen explicitly (the compiler suggests `let`); value-type collections use copy-on-write.

reference-counting.note: ARC with strong, weak and unowned references; cycles must be broken by hand.

pointers.note: UnsafePointer/UnsafeMutablePointer types with manual allocate/deallocate, mainly for C interop.

actors.note: `actor` types isolate their mutable state; calls from outside are asynchronous. Swift 6 enforces isolation at compile time.

async-await.note: Structured concurrency with async let, task groups and cancellation.

macros.note: Freestanding and attached macros, implemented as compiler plugins that transform SwiftSyntax trees.

reflection.note: Read-only Mirror API; on Apple platforms @objc members are also visible to the Objective-C runtime.

compile-time-execution.note: Macros are Swift programs run by the compiler to expand code; there is no general constant-evaluation feature.

regex-builtin.note: Typed regex literals (/…/) and the RegexBuilder DSL.

milestones.event: Chris Lattner begins Swift in secret at Apple (July)
Unveiled at WWDC (2 June); Swift 1.0 (9 September)
Swift 2: error handling and protocol extensions; open-sourced with a Linux port (3 December)
Swift 3: large source-breaking cleanup of syntax and API naming
Lattner leaves Apple; Ted Kremenek becomes project lead
Swift 5: ABI stability on Apple platforms; SwiftUI announced
Swift 5.5: async/await, structured concurrency and actors
Swift 5.9: macros, parameter packs, noncopyable types, C++ interoperability
Swift 6: compile-time data-race safety in the Swift 6 language mode
Android workgroup releases a preview of an official Swift SDK for Android

trivia: Lattner implemented much of the basic language structure in secret before other Apple engineers started contributing in earnest late in 2011.
The WWDC 2014 app was the first publicly released app written in Swift.
Swift took first place for 'Most Loved Programming Language' in the 2015 Stack Overflow Developer Survey.

hello.notes: Top-level statements in the main file form the entry point; no main() or semicolons are needed.

factorial.notes: `_` removes the argument label at call sites; single-expression functions return implicitly (Swift 5.1+). Int is 64-bit and traps on overflow.

fizzbuzz.notes: `switch` over a tuple with wildcard patterns; cases must be exhaustive and never fall through.

higher-order.notes: Trailing closures with the implicit `$0` parameter; `String.init` is passed as a function value.

shapes.notes: Value-type structs adopt a protocol with a computed-property requirement; `any Shape` marks an existential box (Swift 5.6+), and `type(of:)` supplies the type name.

signature.notes: Enum cases carry data; `switch` must cover every case, and the pattern `let discount?` matches only a non-nil Optional. `String?` makes absence part of the type, and `??` supplies a default.

toolchains.name: Swift (swiftc)
toolchains.notes: Official Docker image, verified with Swift 6.3.3 in the Swift 6 language mode. `swift {file}` runs a script directly (JIT) at the cost of slower start-up.

runtime.notes: SwiftWasm can compile Swift to WebAssembly, but the compiler itself does not run in the browser; online playgrounds compile server-side.
